intoxication is not usually seen until a circulating serum concentration of 25(OH)D is greater than 150 ng mL1 (375 nmol L1)
(Holick et al., 2011). In 2010 the Institute of Medicine recommended that to achieve a circulating blood level of 25(OH)D of at
least 20 ng mL1 required the daily intake of 400 IU day1 for children 0–1 year, 600 IU day1 for children over 1 year and all
and adults <70 years old, and 800 IU day1 for those >70 years (Ross et al., 2011). The Endocrine Society recommended that
to achieve and maintain a circulating serum concentration of 25(OH)D of at least 30 ng mL1 (75 nmol L1) required the daily
ingestion of 400–1000 IUs, 600–1000 IUs and 1500–2000 IUs for infants up to 1 year of age, children 1 year of age and older
and all adults of normal weight respectively. Obese adults (BMI >30) require 2–3 times more vitamin D to satisfy their requirement
compared to a normal weight adult (Table 1) (Holick et al., 2011).
